## QUESTION 1

__Use the provided code above to read in the batting table. Then, with Python Polars manipulate the 'results' dataframe to calculate the number of at bats and the batting average for each year a player played. Filter the data frame to only include players with at least 10 at bats that year. Sort the dataframe from highest batting average to lowest, and then by playerid alphabetically. Show the top 5 results in your report.__

Note: A batting average is meant to measure how often a player puts the ball in play and gets to base safely. For this task, use a simplified version of batting average defined as the sum of hits (labeled 'H') divided by number of at bats (labeled 'AB').

The best batting average goes to nymanny01 in 1974 with an average of 0.643 and 14 times at bat. All of the top 5 have an AB of 16 or lower which doesn't give me the most confidence in saying they're the 5 best batters of all time due to a small sample size. The 5th highest batter has an average of 0.5625 which is a larger gap than I expected given only 5 places, suggesting the top batter was at least more consistent than the next 5 when sorted by batting average where at bat is 10 or higher. 

_AI use reflection_

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here

bat_avg_df = (
    results.group_by("playerID", "yearID")
    .agg(yearly_ab=pl.col("AB").sum(), yearly_h=pl.col("H").sum())
    .filter(pl.col("yearly_ab") >= 10)
    .with_columns(avg=pl.col("yearly_h") / pl.col("yearly_ab"))
    .sort(["avg", "playerID"], descending=[True, False])
    .head(5)
)

bat_avg_df
```


## QUESTION 2

__Use the provided code above to read in the batting table. Then, with Python Polars manipulate the 'results' dataframe to calculate the batting average for each player over their entire career (all years combined). Only include players with at least 100 at bats over their entire career. Sort the dataframe from highest batting average to lowest, and then by playerid alphabetically. Show the top 5 results in your report.__ 

Note: A batting average is meant to measure how often a player puts the ball in play and gets to base safely. For this task, use a simplified version of batting average defined as the sum of hits (labeled 'H') divided by number of at bats (labeled 'AB').

Controlling for only players with 100 or more times at bat is much more statistically relevant to their overal quality as a batter. This shows 5 different players from the previous step with a much lower maximum of 0.366 for cobbty01, however he has 11,436 times at bat. The 5th place player has a much lower times at bat of 1,443 and achieved a 0.355 average. That paints a picture of just how good cobbty01 is given his consistency with his incredibly high number of times at bat.

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
bat_avg_df = (
    results.group_by("playerID")
    .agg(total_ab=pl.col("AB").sum(), total_h=pl.col("H").sum())
    .filter(pl.col("total_ab") >= 100)
    .with_columns(avg=pl.col("total_h") / pl.col("total_ab"))
    .sort("playerID")
    .sort(["avg", "playerID"], descending=[True, False])
    .head(5)
)

bat_avg_df
```
